report:
### Conclusion
The claim that conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) supplements reduce abdominal fat is **not strongly supported** by human clinical evidence. While early animal studies showed notable fat reduction, randomized clinical trials in humans demonstrate only minimal, clinically negligible benefits alongside potential adverse health effects.

### Key Evidence

* **Minimal Efficacy in Humans:** Meta-analyses of human trials show that CLA supplementation yields only a minor loss of body fat—about 0.05 kg (0.1 lbs) per week ([AJCN Meta-Analysis](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext)). Comprehensive systematic reviews confirm that CLA’s impact on abdominal fat, waist circumference, and body mass index is inconsistent and small ([British Journal of Nutrition](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366)).
* **Expert Assessment:** The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements reports that CLA produces minimal to no meaningful reduction in body weight or body fat in humans ([NIH Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WeightLoss-HealthProfessional/)).
* **Safety Concerns:** Studies note that higher doses or long-term supplementation can induce adverse metabolic changes, including reduced insulin sensitivity, increased lipid peroxidation, and negative shifts in blood lipid profiles ([PMC Review](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8012289/)).

In summary, CLA supplementation is not a clinically effective or recommended method for targeting abdominal fat loss.
